form.2. SHORT COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course examines modern AI-native software development, where developers collaborate with increasingly capable coding agents. It covers how to define intent, provide effective context, structure development workflows, and coordinate AI tools. Students gain practical experience designing and evaluating agent-assisted software development processes.
form.3. TOPICS / CONTENT AREAS:
Treatment of this list: starting hypotheses — may add/drop/reorder with justification
A. AI-Native Development: AI-assisted coding, coding agents, developer workflows

B. Agentic Software Engineering: MCP, agent skills, tool use, context engineering

C. Specification & Planning: spec-driven development, requirements to executable specifications

D. Software Development Workflows: loop engineering, iterative development, software factories

E. Engineering Practice: automated testing, evaluation, deployment, reliability

F. Practical Development: hands-on coding, projects, emerging developer tools
form.4. COURSE INTENT:
Central question the course answers: How can software developers effectively
design and operate development workflows in which humans and AI agents
collaboratively build reliable software?

Pedagogical emphasis: Practical, workflow-oriented understanding through
hands-on development and experimentation.

This course should NOT become:
- A general introduction to AI or machine learning
- A traditional programming course
- A purely theoretical treatment of large language models
form.5. TARGET STUDENTS:
Programmes: B.Tech. CSE
Year: 3rd/4th year
Assumed background: Strong programming and software development fundamentals;
familiarity with advanced programming and basic software engineering concepts.
form.11. LAB / PRACTICAL COMPONENT:
Lab required: Yes — hands-on coding and development activities

Available infrastructure: Student development machines, access to
AI coding tools/APIs, software development environments, and TA support.
form.12. ASSESSMENT PREFERENCES:
Preferred components: Practical assignments, hands-on coding exercises,
project-based evaluation, and a final project.

Components to avoid: none

Rationale: Assessment should emphasize the ability to apply modern
AI-assisted development practices rather than primarily testing theory.

constraint_notes.note: Syllabus and assessments focus strictly on developer workflows and tool integration, completely excluding general AI/ML algorithms or theory.
The course focuses entirely on AI-assisted workflows, MCP, and multi-agent software factories rather than teaching basic programming syntax.
Emphasizes practical application and developer workflows over theoretical LLM architectures or mathematical foundations.

concerns.detail: The lab plan heavily relies on API access for LLMs and agent frameworks. If paid API credits or licenses are not provided by the institution, students may face rate limits or out-of-pocket costs.

labs.title: Local Workspace Configuration
labs.exercise: Configure local development environments with AI coding assistants (e.g., VS Code, Cursor) and verify API connectivity to local and cloud LLMs.
labs.notes: Ensures all students have a working environment for subsequent labs.

labs.title: Model Context Protocol Server Setup
labs.exercise: Develop and configure a basic Model Context Protocol (MCP) server using Node.js or Python, verifying connection over standard input/output transports.
labs.notes: Introduces the fundamentals of MCP architecture.

labs.title: Context Engineering and MCP Integration
labs.exercise: Integrate custom MCP servers with an AI client, configuring context engineering rules to pass all public integration checks without warnings.
labs.notes: Completes the setup of complex context engineering environments.

labs.title: Constructing Executable Specifications
labs.exercise: Construct executable specifications using Gherkin syntax and spec-driven tools like Cucumber to cover all use cases in a provided requirements document.
labs.notes: Focuses on translating requirements into executable test cases.

labs.title: Spec-Driven Development Iteration
labs.exercise: Iterate on executable specifications to handle edge cases, running automated test suites to ensure complete coverage of the requirements.

labs.title: Multi-Agent Factory Execution
labs.exercise: Deploy and run a multi-agent software factory, capturing and saving execution logs of up to 5000 lines for subsequent analysis.
labs.notes: Generates the raw log data required for the debugging phase.

labs.title: Mid-Semester Catch-up and Open Lab
labs.exercise: Open lab session for students to catch up on pending lab exercises and receive additional TA support. No new content is introduced.
labs.notes: Dedicated to mid-semester catch-up as per regulations.

labs.title: Execution Log Analysis and Debugging
labs.exercise: Analyze execution logs from the multi-agent run to identify the exact step where the agent loop diverged from the specification.
labs.notes: Practises deep diagnostic skills on agent execution logs.

labs.title: Reliability Evaluation of API Clients
labs.exercise: Evaluate the reliability of an agent-generated API client against a suite of 50 edge-case integration tests, identifying critical failure modes.
labs.notes: Focuses on evaluating agent output robustness.

labs.title: Collaborative Agent Workspaces
labs.exercise: Set up collaborative agent workflows using emerging developer tools to prepare for the end-to-end software application project.
labs.notes: Initiates the final project implementation phase.

labs.title: Live Scenario Walkthrough Preparation
labs.exercise: Conduct live scenario walkthroughs of the collaborative agent system, testing against evaluator-selected scenarios to evaluate system performance.
labs.notes: Prepares students for final live evaluations.

labs.title: System Evaluation and Live Demos
labs.exercise: Perform final system evaluations and live demonstrations of the end-to-end software application under three evaluator-selected scenario walkthroughs.

labs.title: Final Project Showcase and Viva
labs.exercise: Final project showcase and viva session where teams present their completed agent-assisted software applications and receive final evaluations.

narrative.course_description: This course examines modern AI-native software development, focusing on how developers collaborate with coding agents. Designed for advanced undergraduate students, it covers defining intent, context engineering, structuring development workflows, and coordinating AI tools. Rather than serving as a general introduction to machine learning, a traditional programming course, or a theoretical study of large language models, it emphasizes practical, workflow-oriented software engineering. Students will learn to configure AI coding tools using Model Context Protocol servers, construct executable specifications from natural language requirements, and analyze iterative agentic debugging loops. They will also evaluate automated testing, deployment, and reliability metrics for agent-generated artifacts, culminating in the delivery of an end-to-end software application. The course is taught through three hours of lectures, one hour of tutorial, and two hours of practical labs per week over thirteen weeks, heavily incorporating hands-on development and a collaborative group project.
narrative.sequencing_rationale: The course progresses logically from foundational setup to complex systems. It begins with workspace configuration and Model Context Protocol integration (M1), moves to specification-driven development (M2), and then introduces agentic loops and debugging (M3). This builds the necessary skills for testing and reliability evaluation (M4), culminating in collaborative multi-agent projects (M5). This sequence relies on CSE201 as a prerequisite to ensure students possess the fundamental programming and unit testing skills required for these advanced workflows.
narrative.assessment_rationale: The assessment mix directly aligns with the course's practical, workflow-oriented outcomes. Quizzes (10%) and midsem (20%) evaluate conceptual understanding of agentic architectures. Assignments (20%) assess hands-on configuration (CO1) and specification-driven development (CO2). The final project (25%) and endsem (25%) evaluate higher-level capabilities: analyzing agentic loops (CO3), evaluating reliability metrics (CO4), and demonstrating collaborative agent workflows in an end-to-end application (CO5), matching the practical emphasis of the L-T-P structure.
narrative.positioning_rationale: This course is distinct from existing IIIT-D offerings. While CSE701 focuses on research and algorithmic applications of AI to automate software engineering, this course emphasizes practical developer workflows and tool coordination. It differs from CSE594A, which covers theoretical and algorithmic foundations of agentic reasoning for scientific problem-solving, by focusing on software engineering practices. Finally, unlike CSE582's focus on traditional software product lines and maintenance, this course is uniquely centered on AI-native development workflows.
